notes: Sample metric_importance_overrides.json - how much a given metric matters on a given instance. Copy to metric_importance_overrides.json and edit.

Kept apart from metric_definitions.json on purpose: that file describes what a metric IS and is the same for everybody, this one describes YOUR estate. A metric worth waking someone for on a production instance is noise on a developer sandbox, and that difference belongs in your data, not in the catalogue.
'scale' declares the ladder once so the numbers mean the same thing everywhere. 0 disables the metric on the matched instances entirely.

'instance_overrides' are matched on the fields in 'match'. Every field given must agree, so a match on db_type alone is broad and a match on ip plus service_name is one instance. First match wins - put the specific entries above the broad ones.
'reason' is required by convention, not by the parser. An override with no reason is indistinguishable from a mistake six months later, and this is exactly the file people forget.

instance_overrides.reason: The application everything else depends on. Availability and recoverability are graded at the top of the scale here even though the defaults are lower.
Developer instances. They are monitored so an outage is visible, but nothing here is worth a page - the data is reproducible and nobody is on call for it.
Finance reporting database. Storage is the failure mode that has actually bitten here, so it is graded above the default while the rest stays as shipped.
